questions.question: Describe a plantation and name the four main crops grown with enslaved labour in the American South and the Caribbean.
questions.expected_answer: A large farm specialising in one cash crop for export, owned by a planter, with a big house, slave quarters, fields, barns and (for sugar) mills and boiling houses, supervised by overseers. Crops: tobacco (Virginia, Maryland), rice (South Carolina, Georgia), sugar cane (Brazil, Caribbean, Louisiana) and cotton (across the South, especially after the 1793 cotton gin).

questions.question: Give four reasons why plantation owners used enslaved African labour.
questions.expected_answer: Profit (no wages, long hours under force); indigenous peoples died in huge numbers from European diseases and violence or escaped; indentured European servants were too few and became free after their contracts; the Atlantic trade could supply large numbers; slave codes made enslaved people and their children permanent property without rights; racist ideas justified it.

questions.question: Explain the triangular trade and what happened to the raw materials produced by enslaved people.
questions.expected_answer: Leg 1: manufactured goods (cloth, guns, metal goods, alcohol) from Europe to West Africa, exchanged for captives. Leg 2: the Middle Passage carrying captives to the Americas. Leg 3: plantation products (sugar, tobacco, rice, cotton) to Europe. In Europe, sugar was refined, tobacco sold, and cotton spun and woven in English factories, fuelling the Industrial Revolution; profits went to planters, traders, ship owners, bankers and manufacturers, not the enslaved.
